title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 233
paragraphs: The Thebans, whose commander was Leontiades, being with the Greeks, had for a time continued to fight against the king's army, compelled by necessity. But when they saw that the Persian cause was prevailing — then, and not before, while the Greeks with Leonidas were making their way in haste to the hillock — they broke off from them and, holding out their hands, approached the barbarians, saying (what was in fact quite true) that they were on the side of the Medes, that they had been among the first to give earth and water to the king, and that they had come to Thermopylae under compulsion, being blameless for the losses inflicted on the king. By saying this they preserved their lives, for they also had the Thessalians to bear witness to their words. But they did not altogether meet with good fortune: some had even been cut down as they were approaching; and when the rest came and the barbarians had them in their power, most of them were branded by order of Xerxes with the royal marks, beginning with their leader Leontiades — the same whose son Eurymachos was later killed by the Plataeans after being made commander of four hundred Thebans and seizing the city of the Plataeans.
